newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Weather smiles crookedly on Argentine crops.
newsitem.headline: Weather smiles crookedly on Argentine crops.

text.p: Farmers in some key Argentine grain zones were thankful after good rains over the weekend but crop lands further north and inland did not get enough.
Months of drought ended in northern Buenos Aires province, where farms received timely falls of from eight to 20 millimeters. Farmers in La Pampa province got 15-20 millimeters.
But the rain was insufficient in most of Santa Fe and even more niggardly in Cordoba, where only a few millimeters fell.
"This will help the maize sowing in northern Buenos Aires and southern Santa Fe. They had some moisture problems which was making them think of waiting and planting soybeans," said a private analyst.
He said the rain would help stressed wheat in northern Buenos Aires recover at least partly.
"I'd say that these rains have alleviated the situation in about 40 percent of our problem areas," the analyst said.

But he said that farmers in central Santa Fe and northeastern Cordoba province may be forced to go over to soybeans, abandoning plans to plant maize. So the government's expected 5.7-percent rise in maize area to about 3.4 million hectares might not materialize completely.

Lack of rain this season has already meant that several hundred thousand hectares could not be sown with wheat. But the situation is better than in last year's harsher drought, when a high-pressure system squatted for months over the pampa plains, walling off the grain belt from rain-bearing systems.
Longer-range forecasts predict lower than average rain and big temperature variations for the rest of this month, but another wet front is due to pass through Argentina mid-week.
"After this rain, the big problem would be if we were to go back to high temperatures. If in three or four days we have 30 degrees (C), the moisture will evaporate quickly," the analyst said.

After a big jump in planted area, traders are optimistic that this season's wheat output will jump from last season's nine-million odd tonnes, with most estimates running from around 14 million to 15 million tonnes.

Their optimism is based on the optimum state of the crops in the southern Buenos Aires heartland of the wheat belt. But an analyst warned that yields are never assured until after November 10, when the last threat of frosts in the south disappears.

The analyst added that he thought sunflower area was unlikely to fall by as much as many are predicting, as changes in relative prices are leading some producers in western Buenos Aires and southern Cordoba to drop their plans for maize.
He also expected the dry weather could mean up to 100,000 hectares of soybean planted on top of the 6.08 million hectares widely expected.
